If one has cultivated the three karmas well in the past but has not yet set them into motion through body or speech in the present, relying on the power of that past goodness, this is called the "hidden capacity.
Although no manifest spiritual response is seen, one is secretly benefited by the Dharma-body; this benefit is unseen and unheard, neither perceived nor known—this is called "hidden benefit."
The response of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is a manifest response;
the response of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is a hidden response.
Second, the hidden capacity [of the recipient] results in manifest benefit:

In the past, one planted roots of goodness until the latent potential was fully realized; thus, one encounters a Buddha and hears the Dharma, obtaining benefit in the present life—this is what is meant by "manifest benefit.

For example, when a Buddha first appears in the world, those who are the very first to attain liberation have never practiced in the present; yet the Buddhas perceive their latent potential from former lives and go forth themselves to deliver them.
Third, manifesting the capacity and manifesting the benefit:

By being diligent and unremitting in body and speech in the present, one can induce [divine] descent; by performing prostrations and repentance at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one can induce spiritual omens.
Fourth, revealing the benefit of latent conditions:

For example, although a person may exert diligent effort throughout a lifetime and accumulate a profusion of present wholesome deeds, these may not manifest as immediate results; yet, there is nonetheless a latent benefit.
"If one understands these four intentions, then every lowering of the head or raising of the hand will not result in fruitless merit;
throughout the entire day there will be no cause for regret. He asked:

Question: "Why is it that some who cultivate goodness throughout their lives encounter evil retributions in the present, while others who commit evil all day long witness auspicious prosperity before their eyes? Answer:
"Karma spans the three periods of time, and its ripening is not fixed;
furthermore, it extends across the three types of retribution, where thickness and thinness counterbalance one another.
The nineteenth patriarch of India, Kumārajīva, said:"
"Because they cultivated merit in previous lives, they have achieved half of the effort required for full realization;

yet, due to some slight destruction of that merit, they turned their minds toward evil, practicing sinful karma with little virtue. Nevertheless, even such persons will first experience blessings before death."
While experiencing the joy of meditative absorption, the mind seemed to attain peace and happiness; yet suddenly various decays and afflictions descended, and the household gradually fell into ruin.
This was brought about by the continuous succession of his own past evil karma.
"It is not that by cultivating merit now one invites such an evil retribution.
He further said:
"In a previous life, one committed evil karma; its transgression constitutes half of the total strength [of the retribution]."
Suddenly encountering a wise person, they were taught to cultivate merit and virtue.
Although they have cultivated such merit, their goodness does not yet surpass that [of others];
with virtue less than their transgressions, they shall likewise die and be born into poverty.
His mind lacked reverence for the Buddha, nor did he hold the Triple Gem in high esteem;
yet after such lapses had passed for more than half his life, his household gradually became wealthy, with abundant resources and many riches;
this was brought about by the continuity of his past wholesome karma.
"It is not that by committing evil now, one invites such a good retribution.
The treatise says:
"My present illness and suffering all stem from the past; [it is not because of what I have done now]."
"Merit cultivated in this life finds its retribution in the future.
If one sees that those who take pleasure in killing long-lived beings are fond of giving to the poor,
and can believe these words without giving rise to false views, [they shall attain liberation].

If one does not understand this, one will fall into grief and regret, losing the correct principle; one will claim that effort is in vain and that merit is lost, asserting that good and evil leave no trace.
However, when practicing goodness, if one remains single-minded without retreating and continues without interruption, the fruits of merit will remain ever fresh.
One need only fear that obstacles may arise along the way; those who have realized wisdom and are wise scholars understand this principle.
Question: "If evil can obscure good, then calamity arises and fortune declines;
if good can displace evil, then obstacles are eliminated and the Way manifests."
Why is it that some who have accumulated merit since birth instead receive residual calamity?
And as for Emperor Wu of the Xiao-Liang dynasty, who placed his reliance upon the Triple Gem—
why was he one day brought to exhaustion and death without any spiritual protection?
"The whole world is in doubt; please dispel this lingering confusion.
He replied:
"It was previously clarified that karma permeates the three periods of time, and the matter is already manifest. Now, to resolve these doubts once more, there are three points:"

First, these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest acts of giving and conduct in accordance with the world, sharing its joys and sorrows; through a thousand transformations and myriad changes, they entice and guide sentient beings burdened by toil.
Some dwell in security yet neglect danger, demonstrating that when things reach their extreme, they must revert;
some abide in glory yet suddenly fall into ruin, showing that prosperity must inevitably be followed by decline.
This causes those who are addicted to splendor to realize that the world is impermanent.
It causes those who rely on their emoluments to realize that life is finite.
It subtly eliminates the defilement of greed and skillfully washes away the dust of worldly passions.

By demonstrating what is right and what is wrong, and by employing both adversarial and compliant means, this is the secret art of subtle transformation—a thing known only to the extraordinary and not to the common or small-minded.
Second, good and evil have no fixed nature, for their retribution arises from conditions;
the power of karma is inconceivable, and its momentum cannot be obstructed.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Karma has three types of retribution:
first, immediate retribution (dr̥ṣṭadharmavipāka),
wherein one performs good or evil in the present and experiences suffering or pleasure in the present."
2. Retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*):
performing an action in this life and receiving its fruit in the next life.
3. Retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*):

"Or karma created in this life may not receive its retribution until after a hundred thousand lifetimes. Furthermore, a sutra says: "There is karma that is painful in the present and has a painful retribution; [there is karma that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant retribution; there is karma that is painful in the present and has a pleasant retribution;
and there is karma that is pleasant in the present and has a painful retribution]."
There is karma that is painful in the present and has a pleasant ripening;
there is karma that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant ripening;
and there is karma that is pleasant in the present and has a painful ripening.
"Alternatively, if other merits have not yet been exhausted, evil will not immediately strike;
or if past calamities still remain, virtuous conditions will instead arise.
Furthermore, if good is abundant and evil is slight, one first experiences pleasure and subsequently undergoes suffering; thus, when merit is exhausted, misfortune arises."
If one has little merit and much evil, one will first experience suffering and later experience happiness; thus, calamities are dispelled and blessings gather.

All of these are cases of retribution in future lives; when good and evil karma ripens, the power of merit in this life is difficult to counteract, such that even those who have severed the fetters and realized sainthood must still repay their past debts.
If even monks such as Sīha and the Dhyāna Master Yi-hang [could not escape], how much less could ordinary beings bound by karma avoid this affliction?

Third, if one’s roots of goodness are profound, one’s cultivation and progress are firm, and one’s resolve is unwavering—vowing to pass through metal and stone—then one will receive light retribution in the present life and be able to sever deep transgressions.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If one has committed much evil and little good in this life, then the retribution in hell will be heavy while that in the present life will be light.
Alternatively, if one has performed little good and much evil, then the retribution in the present life will be light while that in hell will be heavy."
"Even for a person of purely virtuous practice, if they experience a temporary headache in the present life, it extinguishes the suffering of hell for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"May I repay [my debts] with this present body, rather than entering the evil realms to undergo suffering."

"Though a person who has committed evil may appear to enjoy peace and happiness now, the fruit of their actions lies in the Avīci Hell, where they shall be scorched for accumulated kalpas, undergoing uninterrupted suffering.

Furthermore, when a practitioner’s power reaches the point of emerging from saṃsāra, even if they experience slight suffering at the time of death, their beginningless evil karma will be completely exhausted all at once."
For instance, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty served as a monk in China for nine successive generations; his merit and wisdom were always ranked foremost.
He extensively propagated the holy teachings and widely expounded the Buddha-vehicle, benefiting and rescuing the boundless masses, such that his extraordinary achievements are difficult to fathom.
When the time came for his passing, he was lying ill in his room.
The monk Mingzang, who was attending to him, saw two men, each one zhang tall, together holding a white lotus flower and approaching the Dharma Master. They said:

"Since beginningless time, all the harm you have caused sentient beings and all your evil karmic deeds shall now be completely extinguished through this minor illness; you should feel joyful celebration."
The Dharma Master looked around, joined his palms, and finally lay down on his right side.
His disciples asked,
"Master, are you certain that you will be reborn in Maitreya’s Inner Court?"
He replied, "I have been born.
Having spoken these words, his breath gradually grew faint, and suddenly his spirit departed.
"If one clearly understands the three meanings above, only then is one a person who knows the cause and recognizes the fruit;
if one is ignorant of this text, one will spend their entire life in doubt and slander. Question:
"If one cultivates goodness, it ought to be pure; why then would one commit evil?
Since one is capable of committing evil, what use is there for goodness?
If good and evil are practiced simultaneously, I fear that one's efforts will be in vain."
He replied:
"If a renunciant bodhisattva is free from all obstacles, they should practice exclusively in goodness until reaching bodhi.
However, as for a householder bodhisattva, being constrained by worldly affairs and unable yet to attain pure practice, they should cultivate auxiliary paths of goodness as an antidote."
For karma is difficult to shift all at once, and evil is not severed entirely;
one must gradually accumulate merit to advance toward Bodhi.
If one continues to accumulate evil without cultivation, that evil will never come to an end.
One must practice wholesome karma to overcome evil causes.
The *Avadāna-sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a king who, returning from a hunt, passed by a monastery and circumambulated a stupa, prostrating before the śramaṇas."
The ministers laughed at him together, and the king then realized his error; he questioned the ministers, saying:
"There is gold in a cauldron, and the broth within the cauldron is boiling; can one obtain the gold by reaching for it with the hand?"
He replied, "It cannot be obtained.
The king said:
"If cold water were poured into it, could it be retrieved?
The minister replied to the king,
"It could be retrieved."
The king said:
"When I attend to the affairs of state and engage in hunting, it is like boiling water;
when I burn incense, light lamps, and circumambulate stupas, it is like pouring cold water into that boiling water."
"Since a king possesses both virtuous and non-virtuous conduct, why is it that he has only evil and no goodness?
Question: "Is it also permitted for a lay bodhisattva to practice exclusively in virtue?"
He replied:

"If one’s will is resolute and the mind firm, single-mindedly taking refuge as if a deer caught in a net or with fire burning its head, seeking only the gate of liberation and disregarding worldly affairs."
From antiquity to the present day, there have been many such as these.
The *Avadāna-sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a king who greatly cherished the Way and its virtue;..."
He was constantly circumambulating the stupa; before he had completed a hundred circuits, the king of a neighboring state arrived with an army to invade and seize his kingdom.
The ministers were struck with great terror and immediately addressed the king, saying:
"Set aside this circumambulation of the stupa to repel the formidable enemy."
The king said, "I permit the soldiers to come; I shall never stop.
His resolve remained as before, and before he had finished circumambulating the stupa, the soldiers dispersed and withdrew.
When a person possesses single-minded concentration, there is nothing that cannot be resolved.
Thus, even the rivers and mountains lack spiritual power; it is only through human resonance that they respond.
Provided one’s will reaches its goal, there is nowhere it will not be fulfilled.
"As for fish leaping in icy ponds and bamboo shoots sprouting in cold forests, these are not due to supernatural power, but are what the will brings forth.
Question: "If one extensively cultivates the myriad virtues, all are offered through the gate of compassion;"
If one adheres solely to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it will obstruct conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Thus, while in the state, one would neglect the governance of the country; while at home, one would fail to establish a family. Although such a course may be said to benefit others, it does not achieve complete perfection.
He replied: "The Buddha-dharma and its manifold virtues universally moisten all boundlessly;
its power rescues both the living and the dead, and its Way encompasses both the ultimate and the conventional."
When there is goodness within a state, the state prospers; when there is goodness within a family, the family thrives. The benefits are vast and manifold, and the advantage is no small matter.
Thus, the *Book of Documents* says:
"A family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of blessings."
"In a household that accumulates evil, there will inevitably be lingering calamities.
It further says:
"Practicing goodness brings down a hundred auspicious blessings;"
"Those who do evil shall be visited with a hundred calamities.
During the Yuanjia era, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty asked Attendant-in-Ordinary He, saying:
"Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun say:..."
"The Six Classics are fundamentally intended to save the world from worldly customs; as for the essential truths of the spirit, one must take the Buddhist scriptures as one's guide.
If all along the shores of the realm were to be transformed purely by this teaching, then I would sit and achieve the Great Peace."
The Grand Chamberlain replied:
"In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent;
in a town of a thousand houses, if a hundred people cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will become harmonious and kind."
This tradition of moral instruction has already spread throughout the world;
among the millions of registered households, there are hundreds of thousands of benevolent people.
Now, if one can practice a single good deed, they will eliminate a single evil.
Eliminate one evil, and one form of punishment ceases.
When one form of punishment ceases within the family, ten thousand forms of punishment cease within the state.
This is what Your Majesty calls "attaining great peace through inaction."
Thus, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm and fills all of space;
in every virtuous action performed, there is nothing that does not lead to benefit.
This, therefore, is the essential path for establishing one's person, assisting in transformation, governing the state, and preserving the family.
If one establishes oneself by means of this, there is no person who cannot be established;
if one rectifies the state by means of this, there is no state that cannot be rectified.
It brings near the blessings of humans and devas, and leads far toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question: "What serves as the root of the myriad good deeds one cultivates? Answer:
"All matters of principle and phenomena have the mind as their foundation.
Regarding the principle, a sutra states:
'Contemplate all dharmas as being the very nature of the mind;'"
"One achieves the body of wisdom, not through awakening by means of another.
This takes the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the true mind as its foundation.
Regarding the phenomenal aspect, the Sūtra says:
"The mind is like a skilled painter, capable of painting all worlds;
from it the five aggregates are entirely born, and there is no phenomenon that it does not create.
This is the contemplation through mind-consciousness, taking the discerning mind as the fundamental basis.
Taking the true mind as its essence and the cognizing mind as its function:
the function is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind, while the essence is the gate of the suchness of the mind.
Although divided into two according to essence and function, it is in fact but a single mind.
The function is the very substance; the function does not depart from the substance.
The substance is the very function; the substance does not depart from the function.
Although their opening and closing differ, the true nature remains unmoving.
The mind can become a Buddha; the mind creates sentient beings;
the mind creates heaven; the mind creates hell.
When the mind differs, a thousand disparities arise in competition; when the mind is equanimous, the Dharma-realm is serene and level.
When the mind is ordinary, it is entangled by the three poisons; when the mind is sagely, one is sovereign throughout the six realms.
When the mind is empty, the single path is pure; when the mind exists, the myriad objects proliferate.
As an echo responds to a sound, the voice is loud and the resonance great;
like a mirror reflecting an image, the form is crooked and the reflection is distorted.
Since the myriad practices arise from the mind, everything resides within me.
If the interior is empty, the exterior will ultimately not be substantial;
if the interior is subtle, the exterior will ultimately not be coarse.
A virtuous cause will inevitably encounter favorable conditions, while evil conduct cannot escape its corresponding adverse circumstances.
Treading upon clouds and mists to drink the nectar of immortality is not bestowed by another;
lying amidst smoke and flames to consume pus and blood is entirely one's own doing.
It is not born from heaven nor produced from earth; it depends solely on that first thought which brings about this ascent or descent.
If one desires peace and harmony externally, it depends solely on inner tranquility;
when the mind is empty and the environment is still, thoughts arise and dharmas are born.
When water is turbid, waves are murky; when the pool is clear, the moon is bright.
The essentials of spiritual practice do not exceed these.
It may be called the gateway to all wonders, the treasury of all spirits, the foundation of ascent and descent, and the source of calamity and fortune.
Simply rectify your own mind; why doubt external circumstances?
As the sutra says:
"If one performs good, blessings follow; if one treads evil, calamity pursues."
"The resonance of an echo corresponds to its sound; good and evil are like these tones.
They are not bestowed by devas, nāgas, or spirits, nor are they created by ancestors or descendants.
That which creates them is the mind alone; that which brings them to fruition is body and speech."
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
When one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, they immediately manifest in speech and action."
The suffering of transgressions pursues one of its own accord, like the ruts of a chariot following its tracks.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign and the mind is the driver.
When the heart conceives of goodness, it immediately manifests in speech and action.
"Merit and happiness follow one of their own accord, like a shadow following a form.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī asked Mañjuśrī:"
"How can one attain faultless actions of body, speech, and mind?
How can one become supreme, unsurpassed; equal, or unequaled?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas skillfully employ their minds, they will attain all supreme and wondrous merits."
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
"Just as the earth is without discrimination, yet all things depend upon it to grow;
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the locus upon which all objective realms depend."
It is like a person using their own hand to rub and stroke their own body;
or like an elephant using its trunk to take up water to bathe itself;
or like infants who place their fingers in their mouths.
Thus, within one's own mind, manifested objects are again taken as objects by that very mind;
this realm of the mind pervades the three realms of existence.
Those who have long practiced contemplative cultivation are able to thoroughly penetrate it.
"Whether internal or external, all worlds are manifestations of mind alone.

By these words, it is not merely that this is the root of all myriad virtues; rather, it is the foundation for everything from sentient and insentient beings, to the realms of the ordinary and the sage, and even the myriad phenomena within empty space.
It is also said:
"Non-abiding is the foundation.
This refers to the principle that when the foundation is established, the Way arises.
Question: "The source of the myriad practices takes the mind as its foundation.
Within the gates of the auxiliary paths to enlightenment, which dharma comes first?"
He replied:
"Because one takes truthfulness and uprightness as the priority, and takes compassion and transformative guidance as the path.
Because of this uprightness, the fruit is free from deviation; one's practice accords with True Suchness."
"By virtue of compassion, one does not fall into the Lesser Vehicle, and one's merit becomes equal to that of the Great Awakened One.
Through these two gates, one benefits both oneself and others. Question:
"Previously, you clarified that the primary teaching is the direct realization of the true source, while universal practice serves as the auxiliary path to enlightenment.
Now, within this gateway of myriad practices used to dispel doubts and obstructions, I do not yet know what constitutes its central tenet."

Answer: “The Buddha-dharma originally has no fixed tenet; it is simply that, according to the point of entry, one clearly perceives the nature of the mind, which is provisionally named a ‘tenet. Question:
"By what skillful means can one attain awakening and entry?
He replied: "There is a gateway of skillful means that you must enter by yourself."
Question: "Is there not some instruction? Answer:
"The nature of seeing has no fixed direction; how, then, can it be pointed out?
In truth, it is not within the realm of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Question:
"Since there is nothing to which it refers, when one sees clearly,
what does one see? He replied, "One sees nothing."
Question: "How can one see when there is no object? Answer:
"When there is no object, there is no seeing;
no-seeing is true seeing;
having seeing is to follow after sensory dust."
Question: "If that is so, why does the Buddha also speak of 'seeing' in the teachings? Answer:
“The Buddha conforms to worldly conventions; thus, his ‘seeing’ is a non-seeing, which differs from the ordinary person’s grasping at it as a real seeing.
To speak in terms of ultimate truth, the nature of seeing belongs to neither existence nor non-existence; it is profoundly still and eternally quiescent.”
Question: "Ultimately, how is it? Answer:
"One must personally investigate and examine. Question:
"It was said previously:"
Question: "There are no phenomena external to the mind.
Why, then, do you say that 'seeing' follows after sensory objects? Answer:
"All objective forms are directly perceived as the immediate objects (*sākṣāt-viṣaya*) of the eighth consciousness; in reality, there are no external phenomena.
When the eye sees form, no discrimination has yet arisen;

it is only when it instantaneously transforms into the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that it discriminates shapes and images, forming the conceptual understanding of an 'external' object, and thereby grasping them as sensory dust."
Question: "By which consciousness is this object manifested? Answer:
“Objects are manifested by consciousness; they arise through the transformation of internal consciousness and appear as if they were external objects.
It is like seeing the reflection of one’s own face in a mirror; it is not the manifestation of another.”
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Internal consciousness transforms and appears as external objects; due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and phenomena, when the various consciousnesses arise, they manifest as self and phenomena."
These characteristics of self and phenomena, although existing within internal consciousness, appear as if they were external objects due to conceptual construction.
Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have perceived these and grasped them as a real self and real phenomena.

Regarding "like an illusion or a dream": by the power of illusion and dreams, the mind manifests as various external objects; these are transformations of internal consciousness that appear as a self and as phenomena, which, though they exist, are not real.
The Sūtra says:
"Due to the attachment of one's own mind, the mind manifests as external objects;
that which is perceived does not exist, and for this reason it is said to be 'mind-only'."
This is spoken of as the transformation of consciousness when discussed in terms of conventional phenomena;
however, if one deeply penetrates True Suchness (*tathatā*), all dharmas are fundamentally immovable, and thus even the self-nature of the mind does not depend upon transformation.
Question: "From what do these objects and consciousnesses arise? Answer:
"It means that it is established by means of the seeds perfumed by linguistic designations;
though it lacks any real substance, it manifests with the appearance of objects, like illusory things."
Names arise because of dharmas, and dharmas are established because of names;
yet within names there are no dharmas, and within dharmas there are no names.
They mutually constitute one another despite having no substance, and though they possess characteristics, both are quiescent.
Question: "If this consciousness is not established, which consciousness serves as the primary tenet? Answer:
"The various consciousnesses likewise have no ultimate destination.
According to the discourse of the ultimate provisional [teaching], there is only the single true nature.
These deluded consciousnesses are established merely for the purpose of dispelling objects."
When objects dissolve and consciousness subsides, both the subject and object vanish; there remains only the single true consciousness, which is itself the true nature.
The *Treatise on the Three Non-natures* states:
"First, by means of distracted consciousness, one dispels external objects."
"Next, the amala-vijñāna eliminates the distracted consciousnesses, until ultimately there remains only the single pure consciousness.
Question: "When principle and phenomena are unimpeded and all things are perfectly cultivated, which teaching does this take as its primary tenet?"
"By which truth is it subsumed?
Answer: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is interpenetrating and sovereign according to conditions."
To cite any single dharma, the myriad practices are fully encompassed;
this is precisely what the *Avataṃsaka* school takes as its fundamental principle and what is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

As for the six perfections and myriad practices used to achieve Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings, although they constitute pure dependent origination, they are all subsumed within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"If one illuminates the fundamental school and profoundly fathoms the ocean of fruition, then both principle and wisdom vanish, and the paths of words and mind are cut off.
Question: "What is the title of this collection you have presented?"
He replied: "If one were to ask about their provisional names, they would number as many as the sands of the Ganges.
For now, to speak briefly, they are collectively named 'The Ten Thousand Good Deeds Returning to the Same Source'."
There are ten further meanings:
first, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;
second, the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real.
The third is named the simultaneous presentation of the two truths;
the fourth is named the mutual fusion and identity of nature and characteristics;
the fifth is named the sovereign mastery of essence and function.
Sixth is named "Emptiness and Existence Mutually Accomplishing One Another.
Seventh is named "Cultivating Both the Primary and the Auxiliary.
Eighth is named "The Single Limit of Identity and Difference."
"Ninth is named the non-duality of cultivation and nature;
tenth is named the absence of discrepancy between cause and effect. Question:
"Names are established based on meanings, and meanings are expressed through the provisional designation of names.
Now that provisional names have been established, how can their meaning be described? Answer:
"First, regarding the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena: principle is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while phenomena are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Though one acts all day long, there is never anything conditioned;
though one does not act all day long, there is never anything unconditioned."
The conditioned and the unconditioned are neither identical nor different; they share the same source of *dharmatā* and are equal to the realm of empty space.
If one were to claim they are identical, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"All bodhisattvas fully accomplish both conditioned merits and unconditioned merits."
If they were merely one, it would not be right to speak of two kinds of merit.
If you say they are different, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One cannot speak of the unconditioned apart from the conditioned, nor can one speak of the conditioned apart from the unconditioned."
"Thus, principle and phenomena are mutually identical; they are neither annihilated nor eternal. Arising and ceasing are simultaneous, appearing together without obstruction.
Second, regarding the dual practice of the provisional and the real: the real is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), while the provisional is the gate of transformation."
Arising from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no skillful means outside of the real;
attaining the fundamental through the traces of phenomena, there is no reality outside of skillful means.
Constantly merging with this single intent, the two proceed unimpededly together.
Exclusion and illumination occur simultaneously, and principle and cognition manifest together.
"Third, regarding the simultaneous presentation of the two truths: all Buddhas constantly rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma. Why is this so?"
The conventional is the true exposition; to realize that the conventional has no intrinsic nature is itself the ultimate truth.
Therefore it is said:
"If one does not attain the conventional truth, one does not attain the ultimate truth."
Thus, the ultimate truth does not depend on being established to be ever-present;
the conventional truth does not depend on being discarded to be naturally empty.
The two truths coexist like waves and water.
When the water reaches its limit and the waves reach their end, wave and water are simultaneous;
when the waves penetrate to the source of the water, movement and moisture share a single boundary.
"Fourth, regarding the mutual fusion and identity of nature and characteristics, the *Niyatārtha-sūtra* (The Sutra of Infinite Meanings) states:"
"Regarding 'the infinite meanings,' they arise from a single dharma.
What is called "dharma" is precisely the true mind.
From this single true mind, there are two aspects: immutability and conformity with conditions.
Unchanging is the essence (xing), and following conditions is the appearance (xiang);
essence is the substance of appearance, and appearance is the function of essence.
Failing to comprehend this fundamental source, one gives rise to false disputes.
Now, those who disparage appearances do not understand the function of the mind;
those who disparage the nature do not understand the substance of the mind.
If one can achieve thorough integration, both grasping and rejecting will cease.
"Fifth, regarding the mastery of essence and function: essence is the principle of *dharmatā*, while function is the activity of wisdom's response.
When the entire essence is manifested as function, that function is not one;
when the entire function is manifested as essence, that essence is not different."
The function of the very essence does not obstruct its functioning, and the essence of that very function does not lose its essence;
thus, while being of a single flavor, they are divided into two, existing with sovereign freedom and without obstruction.
"Sixth, regarding the mutual formation of emptiness and existence: Now, all phenomena fundamentally lack any fixed characteristic."
They mutually establish and mutually destroy one another; they encompass and support one another.
Emptiness is established because of existence: since things arise through conditions, their nature is empty.
Existence is provisionally established by means of emptiness: since they lack intrinsic nature, they arise through conditions.
The meaning of the causes reveals their distinctions, and according to one's views, differences arise.
To be deluded by them results in ten thousand diverse forms; to awaken to them means that the three vehicles are not different. Why is this so?
Furthermore, take for example a single phenomenon: the Śrāvaka-vehicle views it as real form;
the Initial Teaching contemplates it as illusory existence;
and the Final Teaching regards form and emptiness as non-obstructive, because emptiness does not maintain its own nature but, following conditions, manifests as all various existences.
In the Sudden Teaching, one perceives that all phenomena of form are none other than true nature;
in the Perfect Teaching, one perceives this as the inexhaustible Dharma-realm.
When integrated in this manner, it becomes the wondrous existence of true emptiness.
"Existence can manifest the myriad virtues, and emptiness can accomplish all things.
"Seventh, regarding the simultaneous cultivation of the primary and the auxiliary: the primary is the master, and the auxiliary is the companion."
The assistant is established through the principal; without assistance, the principal can never reach fulfillment.
The assistant is obtained from the principal; without the principal, there is no basis for the assistant to stand.

Therefore, the principal and the assistant mutually complete one another, and the primary and the auxiliary are both fully present. This is also the simultaneous operation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, where the hidden and the manifest arise alternately, the internal and external further support each other, and the vehicle and the precepts are equally urgent.
"Eighth, regarding the single limit of identity and difference: identity refers to the unchanging nature of principle, while difference refers to the adaptation to conditions according to phenomena.
Because it is unchanging, it is able to adapt to conditions;
because it adapts to conditions, it is therefore unchanging."
It is precisely because they are not different that they accomplish differentiated phenomena;
it is through non-identity that they establish a common gate.
If they were different, then difference would be destroyed, for their essential nature would be lost.

If they were identical, identity could not be established, for it would be purposeless. Thus, that which is identical is identical precisely because it lacks identity; that which is different is different precisely because it lacks difference. And yet, where there is no difference, there is identity;
where there is no identity, there is difference.
To grasp at each individually is to fall into the extremes of eternalism and nihilism; to integrate them both is to realize the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, a sutra says:
"How marvelous!..."
“World-Honored One, within the dharma of non-differentiation, you speak of the differentiation of all dharmas.
Ninth, regarding the non-duality of cultivation and nature: that which is primordially present is called “nature,” as it does not arise from being accomplished through contemplation;
that which is now manifested is called “cultivation,” as it appears by means of wisdom.
Through cultivation, one manifests the nature that has existed from the beginning;
through this nature, one gives rise to today’s cultivation.
Thus, the nature is fully realized in cultivation, and cultivation is fully realized in the nature.
Cultivation and nature are non-dual, yet they appear to be distinct due to causes and conditions.
"Tenth, the non-differentiation of cause and effect: the cause arises from the fruit; when the fruit is fulfilled, it then constitutes the cause.
The fruit follows from the cause; when the cause is perfected, it can establish the fruit."
"Phenomena have sequence in time, yet their principle is simultaneous;
they assist one another and repay one another, so that their karmic functions never fail. Question:
"What kind of capacity does that which is set forth in this collection address?
What benefit is obtained? Answer:
"It benefits both self and others, encompassing both the sudden and the gradual approaches.
For one's own benefit, it is the perfect gateway for aiding the Way and the profound mirror for spiritual cultivation;
for the benefit of others, it is the bright sun that dispels stagnation in the Truth and the skilled physician for the two views."
The practitioner of sudden realization does not contravene the gate of arising from nature and is able to accomplish the practice of the Dharma-realm;
the practitioner of gradual progress avoids abandoning the teachings on skillful means and ultimately returns to the ultimate vehicle.
Those who believe in it receive the Buddha’s words;
those who disparage it slander the Buddha’s intent.
Faith and disparagement bring corresponding retributions; the workings of cause and effect are clearly evident.
This brief exposition of a single mote of dust from the ocean of the teachings is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm;
may it propagate the True Path and thereby repay the Buddha’s kindness.
The verse says:
“Awakening is unarisen yet arises; the Buddha-way is unsought yet sought;
wondrous function is non-active yet acts; true wisdom is non-constructive yet constructs.
Arousing compassion, one realizes their identical essence; practicing loving-kindness, one enters deeply into the objectless.”
One practices *dāna* (generosity) without anything to relinquish;
one fulfills *śīla* (ethical discipline) without anything to grasp;
and one cultivates *prajñā* (wisdom) such that nothing arises.
Through the patience of practice, one reaches the state of being unharmed;
through prajñā, one awakens to the realm of non-arising;
through dhyāna-concentration, one knows that the mind has no abiding place.
Realizing the formless yet possessing all marks, Verifying the unspeakable yet discoursing on the means of expression;
Establishing a water-moon site of practice, Adorning a world of intrinsic emptiness;
Arranging illusory offerings, To worship the Tathāgata who is like a reflection.
I repent that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty; I entreat the Dharmakāya to abide forever;
I dedicate toward non-attainment, and rejoice in merits equal to True Suchness.
Praising that self and other as empty and profound, Making vows with equality of subject and object;
Prostrating to the manifested assembly of the Dharma, Practicing the Way while treading upon the void.
Incense is burned to skillfully realize non-arising; sutras are recited to deeply penetrate the true mark.
Flowers are scattered to manifest all non-attachment; fingers are snapped to symbolize the removal of dust.
Generosity is the gateway to liberation like an echo in a valley; one cultivates the myriad practices as empty flowers.
Deeply entering the ocean of the nature of dependent origination, one constantly roams the dharma-gate of illusion-like phenomena.
I vow to sever all defiled afflictions; I pray to be born in the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
Treading upon the ground of ultimate reality, I enter and exit the gate of non-attainment contemplation.
Subduing the demonic armies of reflected images, Performing great Buddha-works within dreams;
Universally delivering sentient beings who are like illusions, Together realizing the nirvana of bodhi.

*The Collection Wherein Myriad Virtues Converge*, Volume II. At Jingyan Jiangsi Monastery: Vice-Abbot Zu Fu; Abbot Zong Yu, Zong Shao; East Hall: Zu You, Zu Shou, Zu Yin, Wen Yu; Dao Gang, Zhen Ru; the Monastery itself: Hui Lin, Zong Sheng, Dao Hong; Guangfu: Benfang: Dao Jun, Wen Liang, Ben Chang; Yuanwu: Yinggu’an: Dao Fu. These individuals assisted in the publication of this work to adorn the legacy of their late teacher, Zhan Yi’an. Furthermore, from various monasteries: Zi Jing and Wen Cheng; and the lay devotee Yao Fuliang of Dahong, who together gave rise to the aspiration for the Way, relinquished their wealth to assist in the publication as a meritorious act. They pray that both in the mundane and supramundane realms, all may diligently cultivate myriad virtues, adorn the Pure Land, and swiftly realize Bodhi.
The myriad virtues all return to this single mind; the vase, the platter, the hairpin, and the bracelet are all but gold.
Benefiting both self and others is the ocean of *amṛta*; encompassing both sudden and gradual approaches is the grove of pearls and jade.
The sincere devotion of the donors has brought forth abundant karmic fruits; the printing and circulation throughout the capital have caused this wisdom to be widely known.
Every word directly points the way to the Western Land; the Mirror of the School hangs high, illuminating both past and present.

In the spring of the Jiyou year of the Xuande era, the monk Deyi noted that this work, *The Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Goodnesses*, is beneficial for spiritual cultivation and truly provides no small assistance.

Those who set their will upon the Way yet abandon this to seek elsewhere are like one who attempts to paint the formless great void or to mend the traceless gale; they merely exhaust their spirit without seeing any achievement.

Reflect deeply upon its meaning and practice it accordingly; not only will you not fail the Chan Master’s merit in composing this work to guide those lost in delusion, but you will also not fail my humble efforts in expending the resources to carve these blocks for printing. I hope you will not treat this merely as something to cover your eyes.
Written by the Bhikṣu Dehai of Liuhong Xingsheng Chan Temple;
carved by Wang Hong of Siming; calligraphy assisted by Xu Junxiang. Appendix:

The Admonitions of Chan Master Yongming Shou. According to the old editions, these admonitions were not included. Now, having been verified through the *Fozu gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), they are appended here because they pierce the core of those in the Zen school with the utmost urgency. For those who study the Way, there is nothing extraordinary to seek; one simply must cleanse the root-dusts and eliminate the seeds of karmic consciousness accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
If you can simply eliminate emotional attachments and sever delusive conditions, such that your mind remains like wood or stone in the face of all worldly objects of desire,
then even if you have not yet clarified the eye of the Way, you will naturally achieve the pure body.
If you encounter a true and authentic teacher, you must with all earnestness approach them with a diligent mind;

even if you have investigated but not yet penetrated, or studied but not yet perfected, these words will remain within your faculty of hearing forever as seeds of the Way. Thus, life after life you shall not fall into the evil realms, and birth after birth you shall not lose your human form;
as soon as you emerge from [the womb], hearing this once, you will awaken to it a thousandfold.

One must believe that true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are the greatest causal conditions among men; they can transform sentient beings so that they may realize their Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
One deeply laments that in this degenerate age, people falsely claim to teach "one Chan," merely learning empty forms while entirely lacking genuine understanding.
Step by step they walk in existence, yet mouth after mouth they discourse on emptiness.
They do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma, yet they further teach others to repudiate cause and effect.
Thus they claim that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi.
Committing acts of theft or sexual misconduct does not obstruct *prajñā*; yet, in this life one encounters the king’s law, and after death one falls into the Avīci hell.
Once the karma for the hells has been exhausted, one enters further among animals and hungry ghosts, with no prospect of escape for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Unless you turn the light back upon yourself in a single thought-moment, immediately transforming the heterodox into the orthodox,
then even if all the Buddhas were to appear, there would be no place for them to save you, provided you do not personally repent, personally regret, and personally cultivate.
If one’s heart and liver were severed as if they were wood or stone, then one might eat meat;
if one viewed drinking wine as if it were excrement or urine, then one might drink wine;
if one saw handsome men and women as if they were corpses, then one might engage in sexual misconduct.
If you perceive your own wealth as being like excrement or soil, then you may engage in stealing.

Even if you refine yourself until you reach such a state, it still will not accord with your intentions; only when you have realized the immeasurable holy body may you then act in accordance with or in opposition to worldly affairs.
How could the ancient sages have harbored any ulterior motives in their provisional teachings?

It was solely because they feared that in the Dharma-ending age, monks and nuns would fail to observe the prohibitions and precepts, thereby deceiving well-intentioned laypeople and causing many to retreat from the resolve for the Way; thus, they extensively established these protective measures.
As taught in the thousands of sutras and set forth in the ten thousand treatises: if one does not abandon lust, one cuts off all seeds of purity;
if one does not abandon alcohol, one cuts off all seeds of wisdom;
if one does not abandon theft, one cuts off all seeds of merit.
If one does not remove the flesh, one cuts off the seeds of all compassion.
Thus have the Buddhas of the three periods proclaimed with one voice;
thus has the Chan school of the world expounded with a single resonance.
How is it that later students largely fail to heed this, destroying the true cause for themselves and instead practicing the teachings of Māra?

It is simply because their karmic seeds from past lives have been tainted; having encountered false teachers in this life, their power of goodness is easily dissipated while their evil roots are difficult to uproot.
Have you not seen the Way of the ancient sages?
"To see a single demonic deed is like ten thousand arrows piercing the heart;
to hear a single demonic sound is like a thousand awls boring into the ears."
"You must distance yourselves from this immediately; it is not to be seen or heard.
Each of you should investigate your own minds with care and never take this lightly. We have stood for a long time; take heed."
